expectedText:
MEDIATION CONFIDENTIALITY (EVID. CODE §§ 1115-1129, 703.5) — INFORMATION SHEET AND STATUTORY DISCLOSURE NOTICE
Prepared for Jane Doe · John Smith

PURPOSE AND SCOPE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This Information Sheet describes California's general mediation confidentiality statute, Evidence Code sections 1115 through 1129, together with the related witness-competency rule in Evidence Code section 703.5. It is prepared by Jane Doe concerning a mediation or mediation consultation involving John Smith, represented by Maria Garcia, Esq., and (where applicable) mediated by Robert Lee, concerning the following dispute: breach of a software license and non-disclosure agreement. Case number 24CV012345 in Superior Court of California, County of Santa Clara is referenced where applicable. This document is separate from, and does not repeat, two other confidentiality documents already in this corpus: the Mandatory Child Custody Mediation Information Sheet (which addresses Family Code mediation of child custody and visitation disputes and the official-information confidentiality rule of Evidence Code section 1040, a different statutory scheme limited to that context) and the Trade Secret Evidentiary Privilege Information Sheet (which addresses the separate trade-secret-specific privilege in Evidence Code sections 1060 through 1062, applicable in litigation generally rather than to mediation). Evidence Code sections 1115 through 1129 apply to mediations and mediation consultations of any kind of civil dispute, including confidentiality and intellectual property disputes such as trade secret, licensing, and non-disclosure-agreement matters that parties often route to mediation. This document does not itself constitute the printed disclosure required by Evidence Code section 1129 (a separate clause below reproduces that statutory disclosure and acknowledgment form for that purpose), does not evaluate whether any particular communication qualifies for confidentiality, and does not represent that mediation confidentiality applies to any specific dispute.

STATUTORY DEFINITIONS: MEDIATION, MEDIATOR, AND MEDIATION CONSULTATION
Evidence Code section 1115 defines three terms used throughout the mediation confidentiality chapter. "Mediation" means a process in which a neutral person or persons facilitate communication between the disputants to assist them in reaching a mutually acceptable agreement. "Mediator" means a neutral person who conducts a mediation, and the term also includes any person the mediator designates to assist in the mediation or to communicate with participants in preparation for one. "Mediation consultation" means a communication between a person and a mediator for the purpose of initiating, considering, or reconvening a mediation, or of retaining the mediator.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "“Mediation” means a process in which a neutral person or persons facilitate communication between the disputants to assist them in reaching a mutually acceptable agreement."
  — Cal. Evid. Code § 1115(a) (Leginfo official text), Cal. Evid. Code § 1115(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=EVID&sectionNum=1115.)
  "“Mediation consultation” means a communication between a person and a mediator for the purpose of initiating, considering, or reconvening a mediation or retaining the mediator."
  — Cal. Evid. Code § 1115(c) (Leginfo official text), Cal. Evid. Code § 1115(c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=EVID&sectionNum=1115.)
  Known gap: Section 1115's definition of "mediation" does not require that the process be court-ordered, court-connected, or conducted by a certified or licensed mediator; its text imposes no qualification requirement on who may act as a neutral. The definition also does not distinguish facilitative from evaluative mediation, and does not state whether a settlement conference presided over by a judge or a privately retained neutral acting in an evaluative or arbitral capacity qualifies, leaving that line-drawing to case law that this document does not address (see the companion clause on this document's case-law limitation).

THE CORE RULE: MEDIATION COMMUNICATIONS ARE INADMISSIBLE, NON-DISCOVERABLE, AND CONFIDENTIAL
Evidence Code section 1119 states the chapter's general rule, subject to the exceptions found elsewhere in the chapter. Under subdivision (a), no evidence of anything said or any admission made for the purpose of, in the course of, or pursuant to, a mediation or a mediation consultation is admissible or subject to discovery, and disclosure cannot be compelled, in any arbitration, administrative adjudication, civil action, or other noncriminal proceeding in which testimony can be compelled by law. Under subdivision (b), the same rule applies to any writing (as defined in section 250) prepared for the purpose of, in the course of, or pursuant to, a mediation or mediation consultation. Under subdivision (c), all communications, negotiations, or settlement discussions between participants in the course of a mediation or mediation consultation must remain confidential.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "No evidence of anything said or any admission made for the purpose of, in the course of, or pursuant to, a mediation or a mediation consultation is admissible or subject to discovery, and disclosure of the evidence shall not be compelled, in any arbitration, administrative adjudication, civil action, or other noncriminal proceeding in which, pursuant to law, testimony can be compelled to be given."
  — Cal. Evid. Code § 1119(a) (Leginfo official text), Cal. Evid. Code § 1119(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=EVID&sectionNum=1119.)
  "All communications, negotiations, or settlement discussions by and between participants in the course of a mediation or a mediation consultation shall remain confidential."
  — Cal. Evid. Code § 1119(c) (Leginfo official text), Cal. Evid. Code § 1119(c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=EVID&sectionNum=1119.)
  Known gap: Section 1119's text opens with "[e]xcept as otherwise provided in this chapter," so its scope is defined only in combination with the exceptions in the other sections summarized in this document's companion clauses; read alone, subsection (a) does not say what counts as "for the purpose of, in the course of, or pursuant to" a mediation, and does not fix a bright-line rule for communications that occur before a mediation is formally scheduled. The rule as written applies only to noncriminal proceedings in which testimony can be compelled by law; its text does not extend the same protection to criminal proceedings.

WHAT SECTION 1119 DOES NOT REACH: OTHERWISE-ADMISSIBLE EVIDENCE AND FOUR SPECIFIC CARVE-OUTS
Evidence Code section 1120(a) provides that evidence otherwise admissible or subject to discovery outside of a mediation does not become inadmissible or protected from disclosure solely because it was introduced or used in a mediation or mediation consultation. Section 1120(b) then lists four things the chapter does not limit: the admissibility of an agreement to mediate a dispute; the effect of an agreement not to take a default, or to extend the time to act, in a pending civil action; disclosure of the mere fact that a mediator has served, is serving, will serve, or was contacted about serving as a mediator in a dispute; and the admissibility of the family-law financial disclosure declarations required by Family Code sections 2104 and 2105, even if those declarations were prepared for a mediation or mediation consultation.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Evidence otherwise admissible or subject to discovery outside of a mediation or a mediation consultation shall not be or become inadmissible or protected from disclosure solely by reason of its introduction or use in a mediation or a mediation consultation."
  — Cal. Evid. Code § 1120(a) (Leginfo official text), Cal. Evid. Code § 1120(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=EVID&sectionNum=1120.)
  "Disclosure of the mere fact that a mediator has served, is serving, will serve, or was contacted about serving as a mediator in a dispute."
  — Cal. Evid. Code § 1120(b)(3) (Leginfo official text), Cal. Evid. Code § 1120(b)(3) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=EVID&sectionNum=1120.)
  "The admissibility of declarations of disclosure required by Sections 2104 and 2105 of the Family Code, even if prepared for the purpose of, in the course of, or pursuant to, a mediation or a mediation consultation."
  — Cal. Evid. Code § 1120(b)(4) (Leginfo official text), Cal. Evid. Code § 1120(b)(4) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=EVID&sectionNum=1120.)
  Known gap: Section 1120(a)'s "otherwise admissible outside of a mediation" test does not itself explain how to determine, for a specific document or statement, whether it was independently discoverable apart from the mediation or whether its only source is the mediation itself; the statute's text supplies the rule but not a method for applying it to contested evidence. The list of four carve-outs in subsection (b) is not stated to be exhaustive or non-exhaustive on its face, and this document takes no position on whether courts have read additional implied carve-outs into the statute.

A MEDIATOR'S REPORT, EVALUATION, OR RECOMMENDATION GENERALLY CANNOT REACH THE COURT
Evidence Code section 1121 bars a mediator, or anyone else, from submitting to a court or other adjudicative body — and bars that court or body from considering — any report, assessment, evaluation, recommendation, or finding of any kind by the mediator concerning a mediation the mediator conducted. The only exceptions the section's text states are a report mandated by court rule or other law that states only whether an agreement was reached, and a report all parties to the mediation expressly agree in writing (or orally under the section 1118 procedure) to allow.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Neither a mediator nor anyone else may submit to a court or other adjudicative body, and a court or other adjudicative body may not consider, any report, assessment, evaluation, recommendation, or finding of any kind by the mediator concerning a mediation conducted by the mediator, other than a report that is mandated by court rule or other law and that states only whether an agreement was reached, unless all parties to the mediation expressly agree otherwise in writing, or orally in accordance with Section 1118."
  — Cal. Evid. Code § 1121 (Leginfo official text), Cal. Evid. Code § 1121 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=EVID&sectionNum=1121.)
  Known gap: Section 1121's bar runs to a "court or other adjudicative body"; its text does not address a mediator's report or recommendation shared only with the parties themselves outside any adjudicative proceeding, or communicated to a non-adjudicative body such as a licensing board, an employer, or the press. The section also does not define what makes a report "mandated by court rule or other law" for purposes of the narrow exception it allows for an agreement-reached-or-not report.

THE CONSENT EXCEPTION: DISCLOSURE BY AGREEMENT OF THE PARTICIPANTS
Evidence Code section 1122(a) allows a mediation communication or writing to be disclosed, notwithstanding section 1119, in three situations. First, under paragraph (1), all persons who conduct or otherwise participate in the mediation may expressly agree in writing, or orally under the section 1118 procedure, to disclosure. Second, under paragraph (2), if a communication or writing was prepared by or on behalf of fewer than all the mediation participants, those participants may agree to its disclosure, provided the communication does not disclose anything said or done, or any admission made, in the course of the mediation. Third, under paragraph (3), a communication or writing related to an attorney's compliance with the section 1129 disclosure-and-acknowledgment duty (described in a companion clause below), and that does not disclose anything said or done in the mediation itself, may be used in an attorney disciplinary proceeding to determine whether the attorney complied with section 1129. Section 1122(b) provides that if the mediator agrees to disclosure, that agreement also binds any other person the mediator designated under section 1115(b) to assist in or communicate about the mediation.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "All persons who conduct or otherwise participate in the mediation expressly agree in writing, or orally in accordance with Section 1118, to disclosure of the communication, document, or writing."
  — Cal. Evid. Code § 1122(a)(1) (Leginfo official text), Cal. Evid. Code § 1122(a)(1) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=EVID&sectionNum=1122.)
  "The communication, document, or writing is related to an attorney’s compliance with the requirements described in Section 1129 and does not disclose anything said or done or any admission made in the course of the mediation, in which case the communication, document, or writing may be used in an attorney disciplinary proceeding to determine whether the attorney has complied with Section 1129."
  — Cal. Evid. Code § 1122(a)(3) (Leginfo official text), Cal. Evid. Code § 1122(a)(3) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=EVID&sectionNum=1122.)
  Known gap: Section 1122(a)(1)'s text requires agreement of "all persons who conduct or otherwise participate in the mediation," which is not the same population as "all parties" used elsewhere in the chapter (for example in section 1121); the statute does not itself define who counts as a "participant" for this purpose (a support person, an expert, or observing counsel, for instance). The narrow attorney-discipline exception in paragraph (3) applies only to the compliance question under section 1129 and, by its own terms, still forbids using it to disclose anything said or done in the mediation itself.

WHEN A WRITTEN SETTLEMENT AGREEMENT REACHED IN MEDIATION IS NOT CONFIDENTIAL
Evidence Code section 1123 provides that a written settlement agreement prepared in the course of, or pursuant to, a mediation is not made inadmissible or protected from disclosure by the mediation confidentiality chapter if the agreement is signed by the settling parties and at least one of four conditions is satisfied: the agreement itself states that it is admissible or subject to disclosure (or words to that effect); the agreement states that it is enforceable or binding (or words to that effect); all parties to the agreement expressly agree, in writing or orally under section 1118, to its disclosure; or the agreement is used to show fraud, duress, or illegality relevant to an issue in dispute.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "A written settlement agreement prepared in the course of, or pursuant to, a mediation, is not made inadmissible, or protected from disclosure, by provisions of this chapter if the agreement is signed by the settling parties and any of the following conditions are satisfied:"
  — Cal. Evid. Code § 1123 (Leginfo official text), Cal. Evid. Code § 1123 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=EVID&sectionNum=1123.)
  "The agreement provides that it is enforceable or binding or words to that effect."
  — Cal. Evid. Code § 1123(b) (Leginfo official text), Cal. Evid. Code § 1123(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=EVID&sectionNum=1123.)
  "The agreement is used to show fraud, duress, or illegality that is relevant to an issue in dispute."
  — Cal. Evid. Code § 1123(d) (Leginfo official text), Cal. Evid. Code § 1123(d) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=EVID&sectionNum=1123.)
  Known gap: Section 1123's exception is conditioned on the agreement being "signed by the settling parties"; its text does not address an unsigned draft settlement agreement, or one signed by fewer than all the settling parties, and does not itself supply model language for a party who wants to satisfy condition (a) or (b) — this document's drafting clause below offers such language as an illustration only, not as an assertion that any particular wording is legally sufficient in every case.

ORAL SETTLEMENT AGREEMENTS: THE SECTION 1118 CONDITIONS AND THE SECTION 1124 EXCEPTION
An oral agreement made in the course of a mediation is not automatically confidential under Evidence Code section 1124, but only if it meets one of that section's conditions, each of which incorporates the definition of an oral agreement made "in accordance with Section 1118." Section 1118 defines that phrase to mean an oral agreement that is recorded by a court reporter or reliable means of audio recording; whose terms are recited on the record in the presence of the parties and the mediator, with the parties expressing on the record that they agree to those terms; for which the parties expressly state on the record that the agreement is enforceable or binding, or words to that effect; and which is reduced to a writing signed by the parties within 72 hours after it is recorded. Section 1124(a) makes an oral agreement meeting all four section 1118 conditions non-confidential outright; section 1124(b) and (c) allow an oral agreement meeting only the first, second, and fourth section 1118 conditions (that is, omitting the on-the-record enforceable-or-binding statement) to be disclosed if either all parties expressly agree to disclosure or the agreement is used to show fraud, duress, or illegality relevant to an issue in dispute.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "The oral agreement is recorded by a court reporter or reliable means of audio recording."
  — Cal. Evid. Code § 1118(a) (Leginfo official text), Cal. Evid. Code § 1118(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=EVID&sectionNum=1118.)
  "The parties to the oral agreement expressly state on the record that the agreement is enforceable or binding, or words to that effect."
  — Cal. Evid. Code § 1118(c) (Leginfo official text), Cal. Evid. Code § 1118(c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=EVID&sectionNum=1118.)
  "The agreement is in accordance with subdivisions (a), (b), and (d) of Section 1118, and all parties to the agreement expressly agree, in writing or orally in accordance with Section 1118, to disclosure of the agreement."
  — Cal. Evid. Code § 1124(b) (Leginfo official text), Cal. Evid. Code § 1124(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=EVID&sectionNum=1124.)
  Known gap: Section 1118's 72-hour deadline for reducing the recorded oral agreement to a signed writing is a fixed, unextendable period as stated in the text — the section does not itself provide for any extension of that deadline by agreement or court order, unlike some other deadlines in this chapter. Both sections' text also does not address what happens to an oral agreement that satisfies subdivisions (a) through (c) but not (d) (the 72-hour writing requirement) — for example, whether it can qualify under the more limited section 1124(b) or (c) pathway, which requires only subdivisions (a), (b), and (d).

WHEN A MEDIATION "ENDS" FOR CONFIDENTIALITY PURPOSES
Evidence Code section 1125(a) states that a mediation ends, for purposes of this chapter's confidentiality rules, when any one of five things happens: the parties execute a written settlement agreement that fully resolves the dispute; an oral agreement that fully resolves the dispute is reached under section 1118; the mediator gives the participants a signed writing stating the mediation is terminated (or words to that effect); a party gives the mediator and other participants a writing stating the mediation is terminated (or words to that effect); or ten calendar days pass with no communication between the mediator and any party relating to the dispute, a period the mediator and parties may shorten or extend by agreement. Subsection (b) states a parallel rule for a mediation that only partially resolves a dispute. Subsection (c) clarifies that the section does not preclude a party from ending a mediation without an agreement, and does not otherwise affect a party's ability to terminate a mediation.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "For purposes of confidentiality under this chapter, a mediation ends when any one of the following conditions is satisfied:"
  — Cal. Evid. Code § 1125(a) (Leginfo official text), Cal. Evid. Code § 1125(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=EVID&sectionNum=1125.)
  "For 10 calendar days, there is no communication between the mediator and any of the parties to the mediation relating to the dispute. The mediator and the parties may shorten or extend this time by agreement."
  — Cal. Evid. Code § 1125(a)(5) (Leginfo official text), Cal. Evid. Code § 1125(a)(5) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=EVID&sectionNum=1125.)
  Known gap: Section 1125(a)'s five triggering events are not mutually exclusive on the statute's face, and the section does not state what happens if two different triggering events point to different end dates (for example, a mediator's termination letter sent during the ten-day silence period). In a mediation with more than two parties, subsection (a)(4)'s text allows the mediation to continue as to remaining parties after one party terminates, but does not specify a procedure for determining which parties remain bound once that split occurs.

CONFIDENTIALITY CONTINUES AFTER THE MEDIATION ENDS
Evidence Code section 1126 provides that anything said, any admission made, or any writing that was inadmissible, protected from disclosure, and confidential under this chapter before a mediation ended remains inadmissible, protected from disclosure, and confidential to the same extent after the mediation ends.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Anything said, any admission made, or any writing that is inadmissible, protected from disclosure, and confidential under this chapter before a mediation ends, shall remain inadmissible, protected from disclosure, and confidential to the same extent after the mediation ends."
  — Cal. Evid. Code § 1126 (Leginfo official text), Cal. Evid. Code § 1126 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=EVID&sectionNum=1126.)
  Known gap: Section 1126 preserves confidentiality only to "the same extent" that applied before the mediation ended — its text does not expand protection for material that was only conditionally or partially protected, and does not address whether a later, independent waiver under section 1122 after the mediation has ended can still lift confidentiality for material covered by this section (the chapter's other sections describing waiver do not specify whether they operate only during, or also after, the mediation).

MANDATORY FEE-SHIFTING AGAINST A PERSON WHO IMPROPERLY SUBPOENAS A MEDIATOR
Evidence Code section 1127 states that if a person subpoenas or otherwise seeks to compel a mediator to testify or produce a writing, and the court or other adjudicative body determines the testimony or writing is inadmissible or protected from disclosure under this chapter, that court or adjudicative body "shall" award reasonable attorney's fees and costs to the mediator against the person who sought the testimony or writing.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "If a person subpoenas or otherwise seeks to compel a mediator to testify or produce a writing, as defined in Section 250, and the court or other adjudicative body determines that the testimony or writing is inadmissible under this chapter, or protected from disclosure under this chapter, the court or adjudicative body making the determination shall award reasonable attorney’s fees and costs to the mediator against the person seeking the testimony or writing."
  — Cal. Evid. Code § 1127 (Leginfo official text), Cal. Evid. Code § 1127 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=EVID&sectionNum=1127.)
  Known gap: Section 1127 uses the mandatory "shall," leaving the court or adjudicative body no textual discretion to decline a fee award once it makes the inadmissibility or non-disclosure determination, but the statute's text does not itself set a fee amount, a procedure for the mediator to request fees, or a standard for what makes requested fees "reasonable." It also does not address a case in which the compelled testimony or writing is found only partly protected.

CONSEQUENCES OF AN IMPROPER REFERENCE TO A MEDIATION IN A LATER PROCEEDING
Evidence Code section 1128 states two consequences for referencing a mediation in a later proceeding in violation of this chapter. Any reference to a mediation during a subsequent trial is treated as an irregularity in the trial proceedings for purposes of Code of Civil Procedure section 657 (the statute governing new-trial motions). Any reference to a mediation during any other subsequent noncriminal proceeding is grounds for vacating or modifying the decision in that proceeding, in whole or in part, and for granting a new or further hearing on all or part of the issues, but only if the reference materially affected the substantial rights of the party requesting relief.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Any reference to a mediation during any subsequent trial is an irregularity in the proceedings of the trial for the purposes of Section 657 of the Code of Civil Procedure."
  — Cal. Evid. Code § 1128 (Leginfo official text), Cal. Evid. Code § 1128 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=EVID&sectionNum=1128.)
  "Any reference to a mediation during any other subsequent noncriminal proceeding is grounds for vacating or modifying the decision in that proceeding, in whole or in part, and granting a new or further hearing on all or part of the issues, if the reference materially affected the substantial rights of the party requesting relief."
  — Cal. Evid. Code § 1128 (Leginfo official text), Cal. Evid. Code § 1128 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=EVID&sectionNum=1128.)
  Known gap: Section 1128's second sentence conditions relief on the reference having "materially affected the substantial rights of the party requesting relief" — the statute's text does not define that standard or state how a party demonstrates material effect. The section addresses only "subsequent" proceedings; its text does not address a reference to the mediation made within the mediation-connected proceeding itself, and does not address criminal proceedings at all.

A SEPARATE RULE: MEDIATORS ARE NOT COMPETENT TO TESTIFY ABOUT THE PROCEEDING
Evidence Code section 703.5, located in the Evidence Code's general witness-competency chapter rather than the mediation chapter, states that no person presiding at a judicial or quasi-judicial proceeding, and no arbitrator or mediator, is competent to testify in a later civil proceeding about any statement, conduct, decision, or ruling occurring at or in connection with the prior proceeding. The section lists four exceptions: a statement or conduct that could give rise to civil or criminal contempt; that could constitute a crime; that could be the subject of State Bar or Commission on Judicial Performance investigation; or that could give rise to judicial disqualification proceedings under Code of Civil Procedure section 170.1(a)(1) or (a)(6). The section's text also states that it does not apply to a mediator in a mediation conducted under Family Code sections 3160 and following (child custody and visitation mediation).

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "No person presiding at any judicial or quasi-judicial proceeding, and no arbitrator or mediator, shall be competent to testify, in any subsequent civil proceeding, as to any statement, conduct, decision, or ruling, occurring at or in conjunction with the prior proceeding, except as to a statement or conduct that could (a) give rise to civil or criminal contempt, (b) constitute a crime, (c) be the subject of investigation by the State Bar or Commission on Judicial Performance, or (d) give rise to disqualification proceedings under paragraph (1) or (6) of subdivision (a) of Section 170.1 of the Code of Civil Procedure."
  — Cal. Evid. Code § 703.5 (Leginfo official text), Cal. Evid. Code § 703.5 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=EVID&sectionNum=703.5.)
  "However, this section does not apply to a mediator with regard to any mediation under Chapter 11 (commencing with Section 3160) of Part 2 of Division 8 of the Family Code."
  — Cal. Evid. Code § 703.5 (Leginfo official text), Cal. Evid. Code § 703.5 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=EVID&sectionNum=703.5.)
  Known gap: Section 703.5's four exceptions are stated as circumstances where the underlying statement or conduct "could" give rise to contempt, a crime, State Bar or judicial-performance investigation, or disqualification proceedings — the text does not state who decides whether that conditional possibility is met, or by what standard, before a mediator can be forced to testify about it. The section's carve-out for Family Code child custody mediation is a testimonial-competence carve-out only; it does not, by its own text, alter the separate confidentiality rules in Evidence Code sections 1115 through 1129 addressed elsewhere in this document.

AN ATTORNEY'S DUTY TO DISCLOSE CONFIDENTIALITY RESTRICTIONS BEFORE MEDIATION
Evidence Code section 1129(a) requires that, except in a class or representative action, an attorney representing a client who will participate in a mediation or mediation consultation must, as soon as reasonably possible before the client agrees to participate, give the client a printed disclosure containing the confidentiality restrictions described in section 1119, and obtain a printed acknowledgment signed by the client stating that the client has read and understands those restrictions. Section 1129(b) applies the same duty, on the same "as soon as reasonably possible" timing, to an attorney retained after the client has already agreed to participate. Section 1129(c) sets format requirements for the printed disclosure: it must be in the client's preferred language, in at least 12-point font, printed on a single page not attached to any other document given to the client, and must include the names of the attorney and client and be signed and dated by both. Section 1129(e) states that an attorney's failure to comply with section 1129 is not a basis to set aside an agreement prepared in the course of, or pursuant to, a mediation.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Except in the case of a class or representative action, an attorney representing a client participating in a mediation or a mediation consultation shall, as soon as reasonably possible before the client agrees to participate in the mediation or mediation consultation, provide that client with a printed disclosure containing the confidentiality restrictions described in Section 1119 and obtain a printed acknowledgment signed by that client stating that he or she has read and understands the confidentiality restrictions."
  — Cal. Evid. Code § 1129(a) (Leginfo official text), Cal. Evid. Code § 1129(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=EVID&sectionNum=1129.)
  "Be printed on a single page that is not attached to any other document provided to the client."
  — Cal. Evid. Code § 1129(c)(2) (Leginfo official text), Cal. Evid. Code § 1129(c)(2) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=EVID&sectionNum=1129.)
  "Failure of an attorney to comply with this section is not a basis to set aside an agreement prepared in the course of, or pursuant to, a mediation."
  — Cal. Evid. Code § 1129(e) (Leginfo official text), Cal. Evid. Code § 1129(e) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=EVID&sectionNum=1129.)
  Known gap: Section 1129 imposes this duty only on an attorney "representing a client"; its text does not impose any comparable disclosure duty on an unrepresented party, on the mediator, or on opposing counsel toward a party they do not represent. Subsection (e)'s statement that non-compliance is "not a basis to set aside" a mediation agreement addresses only that one specific remedy; the statute's text does not state whether non-compliance has any other consequence, such as a basis for attorney discipline (addressed separately in the section 1122(a)(3) exception covered above) or malpractice exposure.

STATUTORY SAFE-HARBOR TEXT: MEDIATION DISCLOSURE NOTIFICATION AND ACKNOWLEDGMENT
Evidence Code section 1129(d) states that if the format requirements of section 1129(c) are met, the following disclosure is deemed to comply with the section 1129(a) disclosure-and-acknowledgment duty. It is reproduced below, near-verbatim from the statute's text, with bracketed blanks for the client's and attorney's names and signature dates. This document does not modify or supplement the statutory text; a preparer using it should independently confirm the 12-point single-page formatting requirement of section 1129(c), which cannot be verified from this document's text alone.

MEDIATION DISCLOSURE NOTIFICATION AND ACKNOWLEDGMENT

To promote communication in mediation, California law generally makes mediation a confidential process. California's mediation confidentiality laws are laid out in Sections 703.5 and 1115 to 1129, inclusive, of the Evidence Code. Those laws establish the confidentiality of mediation and limit the disclosure, admissibility, and a court's consideration of communications, writings, and conduct in connection with a mediation. In general, those laws mean the following:
• All communications, negotiations, or settlement offers in the course of a mediation must remain confidential.
• Statements made and writings prepared in connection with a mediation are not admissible or subject to discovery or compelled disclosure in noncriminal proceedings.
